---
title: "Reading the Coq Proofs"
---

Chapter 30 (@sec-coq-intro) tells the story of the companion **ITC_Coq development**: what a proof
assistant guarantees, the proof-status vocabulary (@def-coq-proof-status), the three active axioms
(@def-active-axioms), and the map from the book's tagged theorems to the Coq lemmas that machine-check
them (@sec-coq-map). This appendix is the operational counterpart: a hands-on guide for a reader who
wants to obtain the development, install the toolchain, compile every file, read the proof scripts, and
query the kernel for the axioms a theorem uses. Nothing here re-argues the mathematics; the chapters do
that. What follows is precise enough to be typed at a shell and a Coq prompt. Symbols follow
[Notation](/notation.qmd); in particular the abstract expectation operator written `E` in the Coq source
plays the role of $\mathbb{E}$.

The development is fifteen Coq source files in a directory `theories/`, built against the Mathematical
Components and mathcomp-analysis libraries, compiling with zero project axioms and zero admitted proofs.
It is released under the GPL-3 license and lives in the repository
`https://github.com/choxos/ITC_Coq`, whose `theories/AXIOMS.md` is the canonical assumption inventory and
whose `manuscript/16_coq.md` is the file-by-file walk-through on which Chapter 30 is based.

## Why read the Coq development, and what success looks like {#sec-coqread-why}

If you run meta-analyses in R or Stan, a fair first question is why you would spend an afternoon
installing a proof assistant to read files you will never execute in an analysis. The payoff is specific
to indirect comparison. Every method in this book rests on assumptions that are easy to state in prose
and easy to lose in prose: constancy of relative effects for a Bucher comparison (@def-transitivity),
positivity and conditional exchangeability for weighting (@def-positivity, @def-ignorability), and the
balance of effect modifiers that an anchored comparison needs (@def-effect-modifier). In a machine-checked proof these assumptions cannot be smuggled into a sentence:
each one appears as a named `Hypothesis` that the final theorem carries in its statement, and the proof
will not close if the algebra leans on an assumption that was never declared. Three concrete guarantees
follow.

- **Assumptions are auditable.** You can read exactly which premises a result needs, in one place, and
  you can query the proof mechanically for the foundational axioms it rests on (@sec-coqread-assumptions).
- **The algebra cannot be fudged.** The subtraction that cancels the common comparator in Bucher
  (@thm-bucher-unbiased), the positivity of the exponential-tilt MAIC weights (the weight form of
  @thm-maic-exponential-weights; its duality derivation is paper-only), and the effective-sample-size bound
  (@thm-maic-ess-bound) are each checked symbol by symbol by a small trusted program, so a sign error or a dropped term cannot slip through.
- **The certificate is reproducible.** Anyone can rebuild the development and re-verify every tagged
  theorem on their own machine; the check is a command you run, not a claim you accept.

What the machine does *not* do matters just as much, and a health researcher should hold onto it: Coq
verifies that the conclusions follow from the stated premises by valid logic and algebra. It does not
verify that those premises hold in your trials. Whether relative effects really are constant across the
$AC$ and $BC$ populations, whether positivity holds in your data, whether you have measured the effect
modifiers: those are scientific questions the machine leaves to you. Machine-checking moves the argument
from "trust the author's algebra and the author's assumption bookkeeping" to "trust the author's
science"; it does not remove the science. For a health technology assessment that shift is worth having,
because a reviewer can see the exact assumption ledger behind a comparative-effect estimate.

**Reader goal.** You do not need to become a Coq developer, and this appendix does not try to teach you
to write proofs. A realistic goal is narrower: install the toolchain, rebuild the development so you have
watched the kernel accept every theorem, open one file, read the statement of a theorem the book tags as
machine-checked, identify the assumptions written into that statement, and run one command that reports
the foundational axioms the proof uses. If at the end you can do that for `bucher_unbiased`, you can do
it for any tagged theorem in the book, and you have gained the ability to audit a machine-checked claim
rather than take it on trust.

## The minimal path {#sec-coqread-minimal}

Before the step-by-step detail, here is the whole journey in a handful of commands, so you can see its
shape. The sections that follow expand each step, and @sec-coqread-trouble says what to do when one
fails. First, at an ordinary shell:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/choxos/ITC_Coq.git       # 1. get the source
cd ITC_Coq
opam install 'coq>=9.1' 'coq-mathcomp-analysis>=1.9'   # 2. install the toolchain (full list below)
make                                                   # 3. compile and kernel-check every file
```

Then, at a Coq prompt started with the project's load path (`coqtop -R theories ITC`, explained in
@sec-coqread-assumptions):

```coq
Require Import ITC.Bucher.          (* 4. load the compiled Bucher module *)
Check bucher_unbiased.              (* 5. print the theorem's statement, assumptions included *)
Print Assumptions bucher_unbiased.  (* 6. report the foundational axioms the proof uses *)
```

**What success looks like.** Step 3 ends without an error and leaves fifteen `.vo` files in `theories/`,
one per source file; that clean exit is itself the verification that the kernel accepted every theorem
(@sec-coqread-build). Step 5 prints the premises and the conclusion, so you can read the theorem's
assumptions (@sec-coqread-bucher). Step 6 prints exactly three axioms and nothing else
(@sec-coqread-assumptions). The companion "nothing was left unproved" check is one more shell command,
`grep -nE "Admitted|^Axiom|admit\." theories/*.v`, which should print nothing at all. If every one of
these signals appears, you have reproduced the book's central machine-checked claim yourself; the rest of
this appendix explains what each step means and how to read what it prints.

## Getting the development {#sec-coqread-get}

Clone the repository and enter it:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/choxos/ITC_Coq.git
cd ITC_Coq
```

The pieces relevant to this appendix are the build files `_CoqProject` and `Makefile` at the root, the
fifteen `.v` source files in `theories/`, and `theories/AXIOMS.md`. The sibling directories `proofs/`
(the Markdown proof catalogue, Parts A through O) and `manuscript/` (a self-contained pedagogical text)
are reference prose and are not part of the Coq build.

## Installing the toolchain {#sec-coqread-install}

The development is built and checked by Coq, the proof assistant renamed the **Rocq Prover** in 2025,
together with three libraries: **Mathematical Components** (`mathcomp`, the SSReflect proof language plus
the algebra hierarchy), **mathcomp-analysis** (classical real analysis, measure theory, Lebesgue
integration, probability measures, and transition kernels), and **Hierarchy Builder** (the tool that
generates `mathcomp`'s structure hierarchy). The required versions, as declared in `_CoqProject` and the
project `README`, are collected in @tbl-coqread-toolchain.

| Component | opam package | Minimum version |
|---|---|---|
| Coq (Rocq Prover) | `coq` | 9.1 |
| MathComp SSReflect | `coq-mathcomp-ssreflect` | 2.0 |
| MathComp Algebra | `coq-mathcomp-algebra` | (with ssreflect) |
| mathcomp-analysis | `coq-mathcomp-analysis` | 1.9 |
| Hierarchy Builder | `coq-hierarchy-builder` | 1.6 |

: Toolchain for the ITC_Coq development, from `_CoqProject` and the project `README`. The development was
checked with the Rocq Prover 9.1.0 and mathcomp-analysis 1.9. {#tbl-coqread-toolchain}

These libraries form a stack, each layer resting on the one below. `mathcomp-ssreflect` is the base: the
SSReflect proof language and the library of finite objects. `mathcomp-algebra` adds the algebraic
hierarchy on top of it, and `mathcomp-analysis` adds real analysis, measure theory, and probability on
top of that. **Hierarchy Builder** is not a mathematical layer but the tool that generates the
*hierarchy* itself, the layered tower of algebraic structures (from monoid up to ring up to field) that
lets a theorem proved for rings apply automatically to the real numbers. For reading `Bucher.v` you need
only the base and the algebra layer; the analysis layer matters for the measure-theoretic files.

The supported way to obtain these is **opam**, the OCaml package manager. Install opam from your operating
system's package manager, then create an isolated switch (an opam **switch** is a self-contained OCaml compiler together with its own installed packages, analogous to a Python virtual environment or a separate R library tree, but covering the whole toolchain rather than one language's add-on packages), add
the Coq released-packages repository, and install the libraries; opam resolves the prover and the
remaining `mathcomp` packages as dependencies:

```sh
opam init --bare                                   # first-time opam setup
opam switch create itc-coq 4.14.2                  # a fresh switch with an OCaml compiler
eval $(opam env)                                   # point the shell at the new switch

opam repo add coq-released https://coq.inria.fr/opam/released

opam install 'coq>=9.1' 'coq-mathcomp-ssreflect>=2.0' coq-mathcomp-algebra \
             'coq-mathcomp-analysis>=1.9' 'coq-hierarchy-builder>=1.6'
```

opam will select a mutually compatible set of versions satisfying the constraints; installing
`coq-mathcomp-analysis` alone would pull in `coq-mathcomp-ssreflect`, `coq-mathcomp-algebra`, and
`coq-hierarchy-builder` transitively, but listing them documents the intent and lets opam report a clear
error if any constraint cannot be met.

One practical point the commands above hide: `eval $(opam env)` updates only the *current* shell so that
`coqc`, `make`, and the libraries resolve to the new switch. It is not permanent. Open a fresh terminal,
or reboot, and you must run `eval $(opam env)` again before building, or the shell will not find the
switch's tools (@sec-coqread-trouble). Some opam installations add a startup hook that does this for you;
when in doubt, run it.

::: {.remark}
**The Coq to Rocq rename.** At version 9.x the prover's opam package may appear as `rocq-prover`, with
`coq` retained as a transitional alias, and the libraries may also be published under `rocq-mathcomp-*`.
If the `coq` package is unavailable on your opam repository snapshot, substitute `rocq-prover` for `coq`
in the install command; the source files and build are unaffected, since they refer to the libraries by
their logical module names, not their opam package names.

In practice, try the `coq`-named commands first; if your shell reports that `coqc` or `coqtop` is not
found, the Rocq 9 equivalents are `rocq` (for example `rocq --version` in place of `coqc --version`) and
`rocqtop` in place of `coqtop`. The two naming families drive the same prover, read the same source
files, and take the same `-R theories ITC` load-path flag, so anywhere this appendix writes `coqc` or
`coqtop` you may read `rocq` or `rocqtop` with no other change. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

Verify the installation before building:

```sh
coqc --version                 # or: rocq --version
opam list | grep mathcomp      # should list ssreflect, algebra, analysis
```

To read and step through the proofs interactively, any of the standard front ends works: **VsCoq** (the
Visual Studio Code extension), **Proof General** (the Emacs mode), or the bundled graphical interface
**CoqIDE**, called **RocqIDE** from version 9. Each lets you place the cursor mid-proof and inspect the
goal and context after every tactic, which is the natural way to read a Coq proof for the first time.

## The `_CoqProject` file and the build {#sec-coqread-build}

`_CoqProject` is the single source of build configuration. It declares one logical mapping and lists the
source files in dependency order:

```text
-R theories ITC

theories/Axioms.v
theories/BasicTypes.v
...
theories/EffectModifiers.v
```

The line `-R theories ITC` maps the physical directory `theories/` to the logical module prefix `ITC`
(recursively); a *logical* name here is simply the name Coq uses to locate a compiled module, independent
of where the file sits on disk, so that the module compiled from `theories/Bucher.v` is addressed as `ITC.Bucher`,
`theories/MAIC.v` as `ITC.MAIC`, and so on. This is the path you will use in `Require Import` (@sec-coqread-assumptions).

Building is driven by `make` from the repository root:

```sh
make
```

The top-level `Makefile` is a thin wrapper: if `Makefile.coq` is missing or out of date it regenerates it
from `_CoqProject` with `coq_makefile`, namely

```sh
coq_makefile -f _CoqProject -o Makefile.coq        # rocq makefile -f ... on Rocq 9
```

and then delegates the actual compilation to that generated makefile. To *compile* a file here means more than to translate it. `coqc` runs the file's proof scripts to build a
proof term for each theorem and submits every one to the **kernel**, Coq's small trusted checking core
(the kernel is explained in @sec-coqread-primer). The resulting `theories/X.vo` is the compiled,
kernel-checked file: an artifact that exists only because the kernel accepted every proof in `X.v`. So a
run that ends without error, producing fifteen `.vo` files, is not merely a successful build; it is the
verification that every theorem in the tree is accepted by the kernel. A clean rebuild is

```sh
make clean && make
```

which deletes the `.vo` files and the generated `Makefile.coq` and recompiles from scratch.

The inventory claims of Chapter 30 are reproducible at the shell. That the development declares no axioms
of its own and admits no proof is confirmed by a search that returns nothing across the fifteen files:

```sh
grep -nE "Admitted|^Axiom|admit\." theories/*.v        # no output
```

Two flaws would undermine the claim that the tree is fully proved, and this one command looks for both.
An `Admitted` proof is a hole the kernel is told to accept with no proof term, so the theorem above it is
not actually checked; an `Axiom` (or an `admit.` inside a proof) is an extra unproved assumption that
every result downstream silently inherits. Fewer of both means more of the mathematics is genuinely
verified, which is why "zero admits, zero project axioms" is a guarantee, not a boast. The `grep` prints
one line per match; finding none, it prints nothing and returns you to the prompt. Had it printed a line,
that line would name the file and the offending `Admitted` or `Axiom`, and the tree would not be fully
proved. The search deliberately scans only the project's own `theories/*.v`: the three classical axioms
the proofs rely on live in the mathcomp-analysis library, not in these files, so they never appear here.
That is exactly why the complementary per-theorem check below, `Print Assumptions`, exists; it reports
the inherited library axioms that `grep` cannot see.

Per-theorem axiom closure is queried with `Print Assumptions`, described next.

## Troubleshooting the build {#sec-coqread-trouble}

When the minimal path of @sec-coqread-minimal stops at an error, the cause is almost always one of a
short list. The fixes are in plain terms.

- **`opam install` cannot find a compatible set of versions.** Refresh opam's index with `opam update`,
  confirm the released-packages repository is present (`opam repo list` should show `coq-released`), and
  re-run the install. On an older switch, `opam upgrade` may be needed first.
- **`coqc --version` reports a version below 9.1, or an old mathcomp.** The shell is using a system-wide
  Coq rather than the switch you built. Run `eval $(opam env)` in that terminal and check again;
  `opam switch list` shows which switch is active.
- **`coqc: command not found`.** Same cause: the switch is not active in this shell. Run `eval $(opam
  env)`; if you have only just installed opam, open a new terminal so its startup hook runs.
- **`make` reports `coq_makefile: command not found`.** Coq itself is not on the path, so the switch is
  not active, or the libraries installed but the prover did not. Activate the switch and confirm
  `coqc --version` works before running `make`. On Rocq 9 the tool is `rocq makefile`, which `make`
  invokes automatically once the switch is active.
- **`Require Import ITC.Bucher` fails with the module not found.** The load path is missing. Interactive
  sessions and scratch files need the `-R theories ITC` flag (`coqtop -R theories ITC`), the same mapping
  that turns `theories/Bucher.v` into the name `ITC.Bucher` (@sec-coqread-build). Inside the build,
  `make` supplies it from `_CoqProject`; outside the build you must pass it yourself.
- **A scratch file breaks `make`.** If you place a scratch `.v` file inside `theories/` or list it in
  `_CoqProject`, `make` will try to compile it. Keep scratch files at the repository root and out of
  `_CoqProject`, and run them directly with `coqc -R theories ITC scratch.v` (@sec-coqread-assumptions).
- **You are on Windows without a Unix-like shell.** opam and the `sh`/`make` workflow assume a Unix-like
  environment. The Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) provides one: install opam inside WSL and follow the
  instructions unchanged.

## Dependency order of the theories {#sec-coqread-deporder}

The fifteen files are grouped into five phases in `_CoqProject`, each phase building only on the ones
before it. The grouping is pedagogical; the binding constraint is the set of `Require Import` lines at the
top of each file, which the build resolves into a topological order.

- **Phase 1, foundations:** `Axioms.v`, `BasicTypes.v`, `PotentialOutcomes.v`, `CausalAssumptions.v`.
- **Phase 2, conditional independence and balancing scores:** `ConditionalIndep.v`, `BalancingScore.v`,
  `PropensityScore.v`.
- **Phase 3, estimators:** `IPWEstimator.v`, `OutcomeRegression.v`, `DoublyRobust.v`.
- **Phase 4, indirect-comparison methods:** `MAIC.v`, `STC.v`, `Comparison.v`.
- **Phase 5, indirect-comparison algebra:** `Bucher.v`, `EffectModifiers.v`.

The actual import edges are tighter than the linear phase order suggests. `Axioms.v` imports only the
mathcomp libraries; `BasicTypes.v` imports `Axioms`; `PotentialOutcomes` imports `Axioms BasicTypes`;
`CausalAssumptions` adds `PotentialOutcomes`; `ConditionalIndep` adds `CausalAssumptions`. The balancing
and estimator layers chain on top: `PropensityScore` imports through `ConditionalIndep` and
`BalancingScore`; `IPWEstimator`, `OutcomeRegression`, and `DoublyRobust` import `PropensityScore` (and,
for `DoublyRobust`, the two estimator files); `Comparison` imports all of `MAIC`, `STC`, and the
estimator layer.

@tbl-coqread-imports gives the literal dependency: the modules named on each file's `Require Import`
line(s) at its head, read from the source. This is the ground truth the paraphrase above summarizes; a
reader tracing what a file needs should trust this table, since "imports" and "adds" in the prose are
shorthand for these exact lines.

| File | Modules named on its `Require Import` line(s) |
|---|---|
| `Axioms.v` | (mathcomp and Hierarchy Builder only; no project module) |
| `BasicTypes.v` | `Axioms` |
| `PotentialOutcomes.v` | `Axioms BasicTypes` |
| `CausalAssumptions.v` | `Axioms BasicTypes PotentialOutcomes` |
| `ConditionalIndep.v` | `Axioms BasicTypes PotentialOutcomes CausalAssumptions` |
| `BalancingScore.v` | `Axioms BasicTypes PotentialOutcomes CausalAssumptions ConditionalIndep` |
| `PropensityScore.v` | `Axioms BasicTypes PotentialOutcomes CausalAssumptions ConditionalIndep BalancingScore` |
| `IPWEstimator.v` | `Axioms BasicTypes PotentialOutcomes CausalAssumptions ConditionalIndep BalancingScore PropensityScore` |
| `OutcomeRegression.v` | `Axioms BasicTypes PotentialOutcomes CausalAssumptions ConditionalIndep PropensityScore` |
| `DoublyRobust.v` | `Axioms BasicTypes PotentialOutcomes CausalAssumptions ConditionalIndep PropensityScore IPWEstimator OutcomeRegression` |
| `MAIC.v` | `Axioms BasicTypes PotentialOutcomes CausalAssumptions PropensityScore IPWEstimator` |
| `STC.v` | `Axioms BasicTypes PotentialOutcomes CausalAssumptions PropensityScore OutcomeRegression` |
| `Comparison.v` | `Axioms BasicTypes PotentialOutcomes CausalAssumptions PropensityScore IPWEstimator OutcomeRegression DoublyRobust MAIC STC` |
| `Bucher.v` | `Axioms BasicTypes` |
| `EffectModifiers.v` | `Axioms BasicTypes` |

: Literal project dependencies of each source file, from the `Require Import` line(s) at its head. The
mathcomp and Hierarchy Builder imports that every file also loads are omitted. {#tbl-coqread-imports}

Two files in the last phase are deliberately lightweight: `Bucher.v` and `EffectModifiers.v` import only
`Axioms` and `BasicTypes`. They sit at the end of `_CoqProject` for narrative reasons (they are the
headline indirect-comparison results), but they depend on nothing from Phases 2 through 4 and could be
compiled immediately after `BasicTypes.v`. A reader new to the tree can therefore start at `Bucher.v`
without having read the kernel-level conditional-independence machinery, which is the technical heart of
the development but is not needed for the indirect-comparison algebra. This is why the worked example
below uses `Bucher.v`.

## What a proof assistant is: terms, types, goals, and the kernel {#sec-coqread-primer}

The sections above were about setup; from here on we read Coq. This short primer supplies the ideas that
make a `.v` file legible. Chapter 30 gives the conceptual account in full (@sec-coq-intro); the point
here is only to install enough vocabulary that the annotated Bucher example reads smoothly.

**Terms, types, and propositions as types.** Coq is a typed language: every expression, called a *term*,
has a *type*. Familiar types are `nat` (the natural numbers) and `bool` (the two-element type of the
values `true` and `false`). The idea that turns this into a proof assistant is that *a proposition is
also a type*, and *a proof of that proposition is a term of that type*. To prove the proposition $P$ is
therefore the very same task as to construct a term whose type is $P$. This is why "Coq checks types" and
"Coq checks proofs" are one sentence: when the system confirms that a term has type $P$, it has confirmed
that the term is a valid proof of $P$. The type whose members are propositions is called `Prop`; so the
line `Definition transitivity : Prop := d_AC = d_AB + d_BC` reads "`transitivity` is a proposition,
namely the equation $d_{AC} = d_{AB} + d_{BC}$."

**The kernel.** Coq splits into a large convenient outer layer (the tactic language, the libraries, the
user interface) and a small **kernel**: a compact, heavily scrutinized program whose only job is to check
that a proof term really has the type it claims. Everything outside the kernel is untrusted machinery
that *produces* candidate proof terms; the kernel is the trusted core that *checks* them.
"Machine-checked" means checked by this kernel. The practical consequence is reassuring: you need not
trust the tactics, the libraries, or the author, only the kernel, because whatever route produced a
proof term, the kernel re-checks the finished term from scratch.

**Proof script versus proof term.** You almost never write a proof term by hand. Instead you write a
**proof script**: a recipe, between the keywords `Proof.` and `Qed.`, of instructions that build the
term for you. Each instruction is a **tactic**. When the script finishes, `Qed.` hands the constructed
term to the kernel; if the kernel accepts it, the theorem is recorded. The distinction matters when
reading: the *statement* of a theorem is what is proved, the *script* is only how, so a beginner should
read the statement first and treat the script as secondary.

**Goal and context: the state a tactic transforms.** While a proof script runs, Coq maintains a **proof
state** with two parts. The **context** is the list of things currently assumed or already established:
the variables in scope and the named hypotheses, each with a name and a type. The **goal** is the single
proposition you are trying to prove right now. A front end displays them stacked, context above a line,
goal below:

```text
  d_AB, d_AC, d_BC : R          <- context: three real numbers in scope
  H : d_AC = d_AB + d_BC        <- context: a named hypothesis
  ============================
  d_AB = d_AC - d_BC            <- goal: what remains to prove
```

A **tactic** is an instruction that transforms this state: it may move something from the goal into the
context, rewrite the goal with an equation, or close the goal outright. Reading a proof interactively
means placing the cursor after each tactic and watching the context and goal change; this appendix
reproduces those snapshots in the Bucher example (@sec-coqread-bucher) so you can follow without a
running Coq.

**Two languages in one file: Gallina and the tactic language.** A `.v` file is written in two languages,
and telling them apart removes most early confusion. Definitions and statements are written in
**Gallina**, Coq's term language: `Definition ... := ...`, `Lemma name : <proposition>`, and the
propositions themselves ($d_{AC} = d_{AB} + d_{BC}$, `forall x, ...`). Proof scripts are written in a
**tactic language**: Coq's built-in one is called **Ltac**, and this development uses **SSReflect** (short
for *small-scale reflection*), the tactic dialect that ships with Mathematical Components and favors very
short, composable steps. So in the Bucher lemma below, the line `transitivity -> d_AB = d_AC - d_BC` is
Gallina (the claim), while `rewrite /transitivity => H` is SSReflect (a step of the proof). When you find
yourself trying to read an equation as if it were an instruction, or the reverse, this is usually the
confusion to check first. @tbl-coqread-vocab collects the vocabulary; the mathcomp-specific notation is in
@tbl-coqread-notation.

| Word | What it means, in one line |
|---|---|
| term | any Coq expression; it always has a type |
| type | the classification of a term (`nat`, `bool`, a proposition) |
| `Prop` | the type whose members are propositions (logical statements) |
| `bool` | the two-element type `true`/`false`; distinct from `Prop`, used for decidable tests |
| `Type` | the classification one level up, whose members include `nat`, `bool`, and `Prop` |
| proposition as type | a proposition is a type; a proof of it is a term of that type |
| proof term | the object a proof constructs; what the kernel actually checks |
| kernel | Coq's small trusted core that checks proof terms; "machine-checked" means checked here |
| tactic | one instruction in a proof script that transforms the proof state |
| goal | the proposition currently to be proved |
| context | the variables and named hypotheses currently in scope |
| hypothesis | a named assumption sitting in the context (introduced by `Hypothesis` or `move=>`) |
| Gallina | Coq's term language; definitions and statements are written in it |
| Ltac / SSReflect | the tactic languages; scripts are written in them (this project uses SSReflect) |
| `Definition` | binds a name to a term or a proposition |
| `Lemma`/`Theorem`/`Corollary` | a named claim followed by a proof; the keyword choice is documentation only |
| `Proof.` ... `Qed.` | brackets around the proof script; `Qed.` submits the finished term to the kernel |
| `Admitted.` | closes a proof *without* a term, leaving the claim unproved (none occur in this tree) |
| `Axiom` | declares a proposition true without proof (none are declared in this tree) |
| `forall x : T, P` | universal quantifier: "for every `x` of type `T`, `P` holds" |
| `exists x : T, P` | existential quantifier: "there is some `x` of type `T` with `P`" |
| `fun x => e` | a *lambda*, the anonymous function mapping `x` to the expression `e` |

: A minimal Coq and type-theory vocabulary for reading the source files. {#tbl-coqread-vocab}

**A hello-world proof.** Before the real material, here is a complete four-line proof over Coq's built-in
natural numbers, small enough to watch every state change. It uses the same three tactics that carry the
Bucher proof: `move=>` (move a hypothesis from the goal into the context), `rewrite` (rewrite the goal
with an equation), and `by []` (finish a goal that now holds by computation).

```coq
Lemma warmup (n : nat) : n = 2 -> n + 1 = 3.
Proof.
  move=> H.
  rewrite H.
  by [].
Qed.
```

The state evolves as follows. After `Proof.` the context holds the number `n` and the goal is the whole
implication:

```text
  n : nat
  ============================
  n = 2 -> n + 1 = 3
```

`move=> H` moves the antecedent `n = 2` out of the goal and into the context under the name `H`, leaving
the consequent as the goal:

```text
  n : nat
  H : n = 2
  ============================
  n + 1 = 3
```

`rewrite H` replaces `n` by `2` in the goal, using `H` left to right:

```text
  n : nat
  H : n = 2
  ============================
  2 + 1 = 3
```

`by []` observes that `2 + 1` computes to `3`, so the goal `3 = 3` holds, and closes it; `Qed.` then
submits the finished term to the kernel. With this picture of state, goal, context, and the three
tactics, the Bucher example uses nothing new in kind, only the same moves over real numbers instead of
natural numbers.

## How to read a Coq definition, lemma, and theorem {#sec-coqread-anatomy}

The development is written in the **SSReflect** proof language, the dialect of Coq tactics used by
Mathematical Components. Three syntactic forms carry the content: `Definition` (an object or a
proposition), `Lemma`/`Theorem`/`Corollary` (a claim together with a proof), and the `Section` mechanism
that scopes shared parameters.

A **Section** opens with `Section Name.` and closes with `End Name.`. Inside it, `Variable (x : T)`
introduces a parameter every later result may use, `Hypothesis H : P` introduces an assumed proposition,
and `Context` introduces several at once. When the section closes, each parameter and hypothesis that a
definition or lemma actually used is added to that object's statement as an explicit argument or premise.
This is precisely the device that makes the development's modeling assumptions visible: a probabilistic
fact such as linearity of expectation enters as a `Hypothesis` and reappears in the final theorem's
statement, never as a hidden global axiom (@sec-coq-boundary).

To see the discharge concretely, take the opening section of `Bucher.v` (shown with two of its results).
Inside the section, `d_AB`, `d_AC`, `d_BC` are section variables:

```coq
Section RelativeEffects.
Variable (R : realType).
Variable (d_AB d_AC d_BC : R).

Definition transitivity : Prop := d_AC = d_AB + d_BC.

Lemma transitivity_subtract :
  transitivity -> d_AB = d_AC - d_BC.
Proof. rewrite /transitivity => H. by rewrite H GRing.addrK. Qed.

End RelativeEffects.
```

Inside the section, `transitivity_subtract` appears to mention no `d`'s in its binders; they are supplied
by the section. The moment `End RelativeEffects.` closes the section, Coq *discharges* the used variables,
turning each into an explicit argument of every result that used it. The statement of
`transitivity_subtract` becomes

```coq
forall (R : realType) (d_AB d_AC d_BC : R),
  transitivity d_AB d_AC d_BC -> d_AB = d_AC - d_BC
```

and `transitivity` itself becomes a function `forall (R : realType), R -> R -> R -> Prop`. The three
population effects, invisible in the body, are now visible arguments. (With `Set Implicit Arguments`, as
in the actual file, Coq may hide the arguments it can infer when it prints these; the underlying
statements are as shown.) This is the mechanism referenced above: any assumption you place in a section
as a `Variable` or `Hypothesis` cannot vanish, it resurfaces in the discharged statement, which is why
reading a theorem's final statement tells you its full set of premises (@sec-coq-boundary).

A **Definition** binds a name to a term or a proposition, optionally with arguments:

```coq
Definition bucher_estimate : R := d_AC_hat - d_BC_hat.
Definition transitivity : Prop := d_AC = d_AB + d_BC.
```

A **Lemma** or **Theorem** states a type (the proposition) and is followed by `Proof.`, a sequence of
tactics, and `Qed.`. The keyword chosen (`Lemma`, `Theorem`, `Corollary`, `Proposition`) carries no
logical difference; it is documentation. `Qed.` submits the constructed proof term to the kernel and
records the result; a proof that does not fully close the goal cannot reach `Qed.`.

The tactics that do the work are listed in @tbl-coqread-tactics, and the notation and scopes needed to
read the statements are in @tbl-coqread-notation. Both are reference cards, not reading assignments. You
met three of these tactics in action in the warm-up of @sec-coqread-primer, and the Bucher example needs
only five tactic families in all, flagged in the third column of @tbl-coqread-tactics: on a first pass
read only those rows (`move=>`, `rewrite`, `have`, `apply:`, `by`) and leave the rest for the larger
files. Three small notational habits recur and are worth naming once: the `=>` in `move=> H` reads "and
then introduce the name `H`"; the leading `-` in `rewrite -E` is a *direction flag* meaning "rewrite
right to left," not a subtraction; and `by t` is a discipline device that runs `t` and fails unless the
goal is completely closed, so writing `by` asserts "this step finishes the goal." With these habits and
the two tables, the annotated example of @sec-coqread-bucher can be read line by line.

| Tactic or construct | What it does | First pass? |
|---|---|---|
| `move=> H x y` | introduce hypotheses and variables `H`, `x`, `y` from the goal into the context | Bucher |
| `move: H` | the reverse: generalize `H` from the context back into the goal | later |
| `rewrite E` | rewrite the goal left to right with equation `E`; `rewrite -E` goes right to left | Bucher |
| `rewrite /f` | unfold the definition `f` in the goal | Bucher |
| `rewrite //`, `/=` | discharge trivial side goals (`//`); simplify (`/=`) | later |
| `by tac`, `by []` | run `tac` (or trivial closers) and fail unless the goal is fully closed | Bucher |
| `exact: t` | supply term `t`, with argument inference, as the complete proof | later |
| `apply: t` | apply lemma or term `t`, leaving its premises as new goals | Bucher |
| `case: x` | case-analyze `x`: split a boolean, disjunction, or existential | later |
| `have H : P` | assert an intermediate claim `P` named `H` as a subgoal | later |
| `have -> : a = b` | prove `a = b` and immediately rewrite the goal with it | Bucher |
| `elim: n` | proof by induction on `n` | later |
| `exists t`, `split`, `left`, `right` | provide a witness; split a conjunction or iff; choose a disjunct | later |
| `exfalso` | replace the current goal by `False` | later |
| `t1; t2` | sequencing: apply `t2` to every goal produced by `t1` | later |
| `[t1 \| t2]` | dispatch `t1`, `t2` to the respective subgoals | later |
| `Qed.` | close the proof and submit the proof term to the kernel | Bucher |

: SSReflect tactics and proof constructs used in the development. The last column flags the tactics needed
for the Bucher example (@sec-coqread-bucher); read those rows first and treat the rest as reference.
{#tbl-coqread-tactics}

| Notation | Meaning | First pass? |
|---|---|---|
| `R : realType` | `R` is a mathcomp *structure* for the real numbers (formally a complete, archimedean, real-closed field); read it as $\mathbb{R}$. It is a structured type rather than a bare set, so generic ring and field lemmas apply to it automatically | Bucher |
| `Local Open Scope ring_scope` | read `+ - * / 0 1` as ring operations on `R` | Bucher |
| `fun omega => e` | Coq's *lambda* notation: the anonymous function mapping `omega` to `e`; here, a random variable as a map on the sample space | Bucher |
| `GRing.addrK`, `GRing.mul1r`, `GRing.mulN1r` | ring lemmas $x+y-y=x$; $1\cdot x=x$; $(-1)\cdot x=-x$. The names abbreviate *add-right-cancel*, *mul-1-right*, *mul-N1-right*; learning the scheme lets you decode new names | Bucher |
| `x ^+ n` | the `n`-th power of `x` in a ring; `x ^+ 2` is $x^2$ | later |
| `x *+ n` | the `n`-fold sum `x + ... + x`; `x *+ 3` is $x+x+x$ (natural-number scaling, not a power) | later |
| `n%:R` | the coercion of the natural number `n` into the ring `R`; write `2%:R` for the ring element two | later |
| `\sum_(i < n) F i` | finite sum of `F i` over the ordinal index set `'I_n`; read it as $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} F_i$ | later |
| `'I_n` | the finite type of ordinals $\{0,\dots,n-1\}$; mathcomp indexes finite sums by this type rather than a numeric range, making the index set a first-class object | later |
| `0 < x`, `x <= y` | order relations on `R` | later |
| `expR x` | the real exponential $e^x$ (from mathcomp's `exp`) | later |
| `{mfun A >-> B}` | the type of measurable functions from `A` to `B` | later |
| `R.-pker X ~> Y` | probability kernels from `X` to `Y` valued in `R` | later |
| `measurableType d`, `probability Omega R` | a measurable space; a probability measure on `Omega` | later |

: Notation and scopes for reading the statements. The last column marks the four entries needed for the
Bucher example (@sec-coqread-bucher); the rest appear only in the measure-theoretic files.
{#tbl-coqread-notation}

## A fully annotated example: Bucher's theorem {#sec-coqread-bucher}

We read `theories/Bucher.v` from its definitions to its headline theorem, the unbiasedness of the Bucher
estimator, which is @thm-bucher-unbiased in Chapter 14. The file imports only `Axioms` and `BasicTypes`
and opens `ring_scope`, so every symbol below is in @tbl-coqread-tactics or @tbl-coqread-notation.

Before the code, fix the clinical picture, because the Coq symbols name exactly its pieces. Two trials
share a common comparator $C$: an $AC$ trial compares treatment $A$ against $C$, and a $BC$ trial compares
$B$ against $C$. No trial compared $A$ against $B$ directly, yet $A$ versus $B$ is the target of the
health technology assessment. Bucher's indirect comparison estimates that target by subtracting the two
observed contrasts, which is valid when the relative effects are constant across the two trial
populations (transitivity). The file's symbols are the pieces of this picture:

| Coq symbol | Meaning in the trial network |
|---|---|
| `d_AC` | population relative effect $d_{AC}$, the effect of $C$ relative to $A$ (the target of the $AC$ trial) |
| `d_BC` | population relative effect $d_{BC}$, the effect of $C$ relative to $B$ (the target of the $BC$ trial) |
| `d_AB` | population relative effect $d_{AB}$, the effect of $B$ relative to $A$ (the indirect target; the file's comment reads "effect of B vs A") |
| `d_AC_hat`, `d_BC_hat` | the trials' *estimators* of `d_AC` and `d_BC` (random variables) |
| `E` | expectation; `E d_AC_hat = d_AC` says the $AC$ estimator is unbiased for its target |
| `transitivity` | the assumption $d_{AC} = d_{AB} + d_{BC}$, equivalently $d_{AB} = d_{AC} - d_{BC}$ |

: The Bucher symbols and their meaning in the two-trial network. {#tbl-coqread-bucher-symbols}

With the picture fixed, we read the file from its definitions to its headline theorem.

::: {#exm-coqread-transitivity}
## The assumption as a definition
The constancy-of-relative-effects assumption (@def-constancy-relative-effects) is encoded as a named
proposition, the formal counterpart of @def-transitivity:

```coq
Definition transitivity : Prop := d_AC = d_AB + d_BC.
```

Here `d_AB`, `d_AC`, `d_BC : R` are section variables standing for the three population relative effects.
The definition names the equation $d_{AC} = d_{AB} + d_{BC}$; nothing is asserted, the name simply
abbreviates the proposition so later results can take it as a hypothesis. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#exm-coqread-subtract}
## A lemma and its proof
The equivalent subtractive form (@prp-transitivity-consistency) is a one-line lemma:

```coq
Lemma transitivity_subtract :
  transitivity -> d_AB = d_AC - d_BC.
Proof.
  rewrite /transitivity => H.
  by rewrite H GRing.addrK.
Qed.
```

The statement reads: *if `transitivity` holds, then $d_{AB} = d_{AC} - d_{BC}$.* The proof has two steps.
`rewrite /transitivity` unfolds the definition, so the antecedent to be introduced becomes the explicit
equation $d_{AC} = d_{AB} + d_{BC}$, and `=> H` introduces it into the context under the name `H`. Then
`by rewrite H GRing.addrK` rewrites the goal's $d_{AC}$ to $d_{AB} + d_{BC}$ using `H`, after which
`GRing.addrK` (the cancellation law $x + y - y = x$) collapses $(d_{AB} + d_{BC}) - d_{BC}$ to $d_{AB}$;
`by` certifies that the goal is now closed.

Watching the state makes this concrete. The proof opens with the implication as the goal:

```text
  R : realType
  d_AB, d_AC, d_BC : R
  ============================
  transitivity -> d_AB = d_AC - d_BC
```

`rewrite /transitivity` unfolds the name, and `=> H` moves the (now explicit) antecedent into the context:

```text
  H : d_AC = d_AB + d_BC
  ============================
  d_AB = d_AC - d_BC
```

`rewrite H` replaces `d_AC` by `d_AB + d_BC` in the goal, and `GRing.addrK` cancels the trailing `- d_BC`,
reducing the goal to `d_AB = d_AB`, which `by` closes:

```text
  after rewrite H:      d_AB = d_AB + d_BC - d_BC
  after GRing.addrK:    d_AB = d_AB            (closed by reflexivity)
```

$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#exm-coqread-expectation}
## The abstract expectation operator
Unbiasedness is stated over an abstract expectation. The trial estimators are random variables on a
common probability space, and the expectation is a section variable whose only assumed property is
linearity, supplied as a hypothesis:

```coq
Variable (E : (Omega -> R) -> R).

Hypothesis E_linearity :
  forall (X Y : Omega -> R) (a b : R),
  E (fun omega => a * X omega + b * Y omega) = a * E X + b * E Y.
```

Read the type slowly. A value of type `Omega -> R` is a function from the sample space `Omega` to the
reals, which is exactly a random variable: it assigns a number to each possible world `omega`. So
`E : (Omega -> R) -> R` is a function that eats a random variable and returns a real number, the role of
the expectation $\mathbb{E}$ in the [Notation](/notation.qmd). The hypothesis's opening
`forall (X Y : Omega -> R) (a b : R), ...` reads "for all random variables `X`, `Y` and all reals `a`,
`b`," and its body is the linearity identity $\mathbb{E}[aX + bY] = a\,\mathbb{E}[X] + b\,\mathbb{E}[Y]$. `E_linearity` is the formal counterpart of linearity of expectation (A.4 in
the proof catalogue); making it a `Hypothesis` rather than building a specific integral is the
"abstract-operator" pattern (@sec-coq-structure) that lets the algebra of estimands be machine-checked
without committing to an integration theory. This is not merely a convenience for the formalizer: in
population adjustment we manipulate expectations and conditional expectations constantly without ever
specifying the underlying measure, and the unbiasedness proofs for Bucher, MAIC, and STC all turn on
linearity alone. Assuming exactly linearity, and nothing more, is therefore faithful to how these
arguments actually run on paper. From it the file derives the difference rule:

```coq
Lemma E_sub (X Y : Omega -> R) :
  E (fun omega => X omega - Y omega) = E X - E Y.
Proof.
  have -> : (fun omega => X omega - Y omega)
         = (fun omega => 1 * X omega + (-1) * Y omega).
    apply: fun_ext => omega.
    by rewrite GRing.mul1r GRing.mulN1r.
  rewrite E_linearity GRing.mul1r GRing.mulN1r.
  by [].
Qed.
```

This proof introduces two constructs worth slowing down on. `have -> : A = B` does two things at once:
it opens a *subgoal* to prove the equation `A = B`, and once that subgoal is closed it immediately
rewrites the main goal with it. Here `A` is the integrand `fun omega => X omega - Y omega` and `B` is
`fun omega => 1 * X omega + (-1) * Y omega`, so the first task is to prove these two functions equal:

```text
  ============================
  (fun omega => X omega - Y omega) = (fun omega => 1 * X omega + (-1) * Y omega)
```

Two functions are equal when they agree on every input; that principle is **functional extensionality**,
and in this development it is the lemma `fun_ext` from `Axioms.v`. `apply: fun_ext` reduces the
function-equality subgoal to a pointwise one, and `=> omega` names the input, leaving an ordinary ring
equation:

```text
  omega : Omega
  ============================
  X omega - Y omega = 1 * X omega + (-1) * Y omega
```

The ring rewrites $1\cdot x = x$ (`GRing.mul1r`) and $(-1)\cdot x = -x$ (`GRing.mulN1r`) close it. Back in
the main goal, the integrand is now the linear combination, so `rewrite E_linearity` applies linearity
with $a = 1$, $b = -1$; the same two ring rewrites simplify the coefficients, leaving $E\,X - E\,Y$, and
`by []` closes. The lemma is exactly linearity of expectation specialized to a difference, and it is the
only fact about `E` that Bucher's theorem will need. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#exm-coqread-bucher-thm}
## The theorem
The headline result, the formal @thm-bucher-unbiased, is now three lines:

```coq
Theorem bucher_unbiased (d_AB d_AC d_BC : R) :
  E d_AC_hat = d_AC ->
  E d_BC_hat = d_BC ->
  d_AB = d_AC - d_BC ->
  E (fun omega => d_AC_hat omega - d_BC_hat omega) = d_AB.
Proof.
  move=> H_AC H_BC H_trans.
  rewrite E_sub H_AC H_BC.
  by rewrite H_trans.
Qed.
```

Read the statement top to bottom. The three premises are: `E d_AC_hat = d_AC`, that the $AC$ trial
estimator is unbiased for $d_{AC}$; `E d_BC_hat = d_BC`, likewise for the $BC$ trial (these two are the
formal content of @prp-trial-unbiased); and `d_AB = d_AC - d_BC`, the constancy assumption in subtractive
form (@exm-coqread-transitivity). The conclusion is that the expectation of the difference of the two
estimators equals the target $d_{AB}$, that is, the Bucher estimator is unbiased.

The proof introduces the three premises as `H_AC`, `H_BC`, `H_trans` with `move=>`. Then `rewrite E_sub`
turns the goal's left side $E[d_{AC}\text{-hat} - d_{BC}\text{-hat}]$ into
$E\,d_{AC}\text{-hat} - E\,d_{BC}\text{-hat}$, and the same `rewrite` continues with `H_AC` and `H_BC` to
replace those two expectations by $d_{AC}$ and $d_{BC}$, leaving the goal $d_{AC} - d_{BC} = d_{AB}$.
Finally `by rewrite H_trans` rewrites $d_{AB}$ to $d_{AC} - d_{BC}$ and closes.

In state snapshots, after `move=> H_AC H_BC H_trans` the three premises sit in the context and the goal
is the bare conclusion:

```text
  H_AC : E d_AC_hat = d_AC
  H_BC : E d_BC_hat = d_BC
  H_trans : d_AB = d_AC - d_BC
  ============================
  E (fun omega => d_AC_hat omega - d_BC_hat omega) = d_AB
```

The chained `rewrite E_sub H_AC H_BC` applies three equations left to right in turn, and the goal shrinks
at each step:

```text
  after E_sub:   E d_AC_hat - E d_BC_hat = d_AB
  after H_AC:    d_AC - E d_BC_hat = d_AB
  after H_BC:    d_AC - d_BC = d_AB
```

One point of rewrite direction is worth naming, since it is a common first-time snag. `rewrite H_trans`
uses `H_trans : d_AB = d_AC - d_BC` left to right: it looks for the left side `d_AB` in the goal and
replaces it with the right side `d_AC - d_BC`. The goal is `d_AC - d_BC = d_AB`, whose only `d_AB` is on
the right, so it becomes `d_AC - d_BC = d_AC - d_BC`, which closes by reflexivity. To rewrite the other
way, replacing `d_AC - d_BC` by `d_AB`, one would write `rewrite -H_trans` with the leading minus, the
SSReflect direction flag (not a subtraction).

The only structural property of `E` used anywhere is linearity, through `E_sub`; this is why the abstract
operator suffices.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The same file continues with `bucher_variance`, the additivity of variances under zero covariance
(@thm-bucher-variance), proved by the identical pattern over abstract `Var` and `Cov` operators with the
variance-of-a-difference rule supplied as a hypothesis.

## Inspecting the active axioms {#sec-coqread-assumptions}

The decisive question a proof assistant can answer that a paper proof cannot is: *which axioms does this
finished theorem actually use?* The command is `Print Assumptions`. It traverses the kernel proof term
and reports every axiom and unproved constant the theorem transitively depends on. To run it, compile the
tree (@sec-coqread-build), then load the relevant module by its logical name and query the theorem.

::: {.remark}
**Two kinds of assumption, before you read the output.** A theorem depends on two different things, and
`Print Assumptions` reports only the second. The first kind is its *ordinary premises*: the modeling
assumptions written into the statement, such as unbiasedness of an estimator or constancy of relative
effects. You read those by reading the statement (`Check` prints it). The second kind is the *foundational
axioms*: logical principles the proof term rests on, below the level of any particular theorem.
`Print Assumptions` prints the second kind only. So the question "what does this proof rest on" has two
halves: read the statement for the scientific premises, then run `Print Assumptions` for the logical
axioms. Keep both in view; neither alone is the full picture (@def-coq-proof-status). $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

Interactively, start a Coq top level with the project's load path and issue the commands:

```sh
coqtop -R theories ITC          # or: rocqtop -R theories ITC
```

```coq
Require Import ITC.MAIC.
Print Assumptions ESS_upper_bound.
```

Equivalently, in batch mode, place a scratch file at the repository root (anywhere outside the
`_CoqProject` file list, so `make` ignores it) and run it through the compiler with the same load path. The scratch file holds exactly the two commands
you would otherwise type interactively:

```coq
(* scratch.v *)
Require Import ITC.MAIC.
Print Assumptions ESS_upper_bound.
```

```sh
coqc -R theories ITC scratch.v        # prints the assumptions report to the terminal
```

For the effective-sample-size bound the output is exactly the three classical axioms inherited from
mathcomp-analysis and nothing else:

```text
Axioms:
boolp.propositional_extensionality : forall P Q : Prop, P <-> Q -> P = Q
boolp.functional_extensionality_dep :
  forall (A : Type) (B : A -> Type) (f g : forall x : A, B x),
  (forall x : A, f x = g x) -> f = g
boolp.constructive_indefinite_description :
  forall (A : Type) (P : A -> Prop), (exists x : A, P x) -> {x : A | P x}
```

These are the three active axioms catalogued in @def-active-axioms; for what they mean and why they are
uncontroversial, see @sec-coq-axioms.

@tbl-coqread-axioms gives a one-line reading of each, so you can interpret the output without leaving the
page:

| Printed axiom | Plain reading |
|---|---|
| `propositional_extensionality` | two propositions that imply each other are *equal*, so logically equivalent statements can be interchanged |
| `functional_extensionality_dep` | two functions that agree on every input are equal (this is the `fun_ext` used in `E_sub`) |
| `constructive_indefinite_description` | from a proof that some `x` exists, one may *name* such an `x`; a form of the axiom of choice |

: Plain reading of the three classical axioms mathcomp-analysis supplies, which every tagged theorem in
the tree inherits, and no others. {#tbl-coqread-axioms}

The same query on `bucher_unbiased`, `cauchy_schwarz_ones`,
`not_EM_does_not_imply_not_PV`, `propensity_score_is_balancing`, and `double_robustness` returns the
identical three-line list: no project axiom, no admitted lemma, no hidden assumption. The absence of the
law of the excluded middle from the list is not an omission; it is a derived theorem (`EM`, via
Diaconescu's argument from the three axioms above), so a proof that uses classical case analysis adds no
fourth axiom.

To see the sameness rather than take it on trust, run the same query on the Bucher theorem you read in
@sec-coqread-bucher:

```coq
Require Import ITC.Bucher.
Print Assumptions bucher_unbiased.
```

```text
Axioms:
boolp.propositional_extensionality : forall P Q : Prop, P <-> Q -> P = Q
boolp.functional_extensionality_dep :
  forall (A : Type) (B : A -> Type) (f g : forall x : A, B x),
  (forall x : A, f x = g x) -> f = g
boolp.constructive_indefinite_description :
  forall (A : Type) (P : A -> Prop), (exists x : A, P x) -> {x : A | P x}
```

The list is character for character the one produced for `ESS_upper_bound`: the same three classical
axioms, and nothing added by the indirect-comparison algebra.

::: {.remark}
**Reading a theorem's premises versus its axioms.** `Print Assumptions` reports only the foundational
axioms, not the named section hypotheses. A theorem such as `mu1_IPW_unbiased` carries the tower-property
premise `Hipw1` as an explicit argument in its *statement* (the boundary policy of @sec-coq-boundary);
that premise is visible by reading the statement, while `Print Assumptions` confirms that, beyond it, the
proof rests on nothing but the three classical axioms. The Bucher theorem you just queried makes the same point concretely. Its *statement*, printed by `Check
bucher_unbiased`, lists three premises: `E d_AC_hat = d_AC`, `E d_BC_hat = d_BC`, and
`d_AB = d_AC - d_BC`. Those are the scientific assumptions, the unbiasedness of each trial estimator and
the constancy of relative effects, and they are what a health technology assessment must defend. Its
`Print Assumptions` output, shown above, lists three classical axioms and nothing more. The first triple
tells you what the theorem assumes about the world; the second tells you what it assumes about logic; the
theorem is unconditionally true given the first, resting on nothing but the second.

The two readings together are what @def-coq-proof-status calls the two-level reading. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

Four further commands are useful while reading. `Check t` prints the type of a term or the statement of a
lemma; `About name` prints a lemma's statement together with its arguments and how they are inferred;
`Print name` prints the body of a definition; `Search pat` finds lemmas whose statement matches a
pattern, for example `Search _ (_ + _ - _)` to find cancellation lemmas; and `Locate "++"` resolves a
notation to the constant it denotes. Stepping through a proof in VsCoq, Proof General, or RocqIDE and
watching the goal change after each tactic is, in practice, the fastest way to understand a script.

As a reading aid, `Check` prints a theorem's statement without opening the file. For `bucher_unbiased`
its output begins with the section parameters it discharges (the space `Omega`, the estimators, the
operator `E`, and the linearity hypothesis) and ends with the operative part:

```text
  ... ->
  forall d_AB d_AC d_BC : R,
    E d_AC_hat = d_AC ->
    E d_BC_hat = d_BC ->
    d_AB = d_AC - d_BC ->
    E (fun omega => d_AC_hat omega - d_BC_hat omega) = d_AB
```

The premises and conclusion appear exactly as in the source, so `Check` alone is often enough to audit
what a tagged theorem assumes.

: The fifteen source files of `theories/`, with headline results and the book slugs they machine-check.
Phase numbers are from @sec-coqread-deporder. {#tbl-coqread-files}

Read this as a route, not only an index. If your aim is ITC intuition rather than the measure-theoretic
core, take the files in increasing order of difficulty and centrality, not in `_CoqProject` order. Start
with `Bucher.v` (the worked example above; it depends only on Phase 1). Then read `EffectModifiers.v`,
which has the same light dependencies and is closer to the heart of population adjustment, since it is
where the distinction between effect modifiers and prognostic variables is made precise. Then `MAIC.v`
and `STC.v`, the two population-adjustment methods, and `Comparison.v`, which contrasts them. Defer
`ConditionalIndep.v`, `BalancingScore.v`, and `PropensityScore.v` until the causal-inference concepts of
Chapters 9 and 10 are secure; they are the technical foundation but the steepest reading. The estimator
files `IPWEstimator.v`, `OutcomeRegression.v`, and `DoublyRobust.v` are most rewarding after Chapter 10.
A reader who only wants to confirm the headline indirect-comparison results can stop after `Bucher.v`,
`MAIC.v`, and `EffectModifiers.v`.

## Notes and references {#sec-coqread-notes}

This appendix is the hands-on companion to Chapter 30, which gives the conceptual account of the
formalization: what a proof assistant does and does not certify (@sec-coq-guarantees), the proof-status
tiers (@def-coq-proof-status), the active axioms and why they are benign (@def-active-axioms), the
named-hypothesis boundary and the discrete model (@sec-coq-boundary), and the full book-to-Coq map
(@sec-coq-map). The worked example of @sec-coq-worked traces the effective-sample-size bound to the
kernel; the complementary worked example here (@sec-coqread-bucher) reads the Bucher unbiasedness proof
line by line, since `Bucher.v` is the file that established the abstract-operator pattern and depends only
on the Phase 1 foundations.

All file names, module paths, build commands, and Coq lemma names were read from the ITC_Coq repository
(`_CoqProject`, `Makefile`, `theories/AXIOMS.md`, and the fifteen `theories/*.v` files) and from the
project `README`. The toolchain versions are those declared there: Coq (Rocq Prover) 9.1 or later,
mathcomp-ssreflect 2.0 or later, mathcomp-analysis 1.9 or later, and Hierarchy Builder 1.6 or later, with
the development checked under the Rocq Prover 9.1.0. The opam workflow is the standard installation route
for the Coq ecosystem.

The mathematics formalized in the tree is attributed in its home chapters: the potential-outcomes
calculus and the g-formula in the tradition surveyed by @hernan2020whatif; the propensity score and the
balancing theorems to @rosenbaum1983; inverse probability weighting and doubly robust estimation to
@robins1994 and @bangrobins2005; the indirect comparison to @bucher1997; matching-adjusted indirect
comparison to @signorovitch2010maic, with the effective-sample-size formula and its bound as Eq. (6.1) of
@phillippo2019thesis; and simulated treatment comparison to @caro2010stc. The placement of all of this
within the population-adjustment framework follows @phillippo2019thesis. There is no machine-checked
counterpart for this appendix itself; it is a guide to running and reading the proofs that machine-check
the results tagged throughout the book.

**Where to go next.** Once you can read `Bucher.v`, the natural progression stays within the
light-dependency files before touching the measure-theoretic core: `EffectModifiers.v` next, for the
effect-modifier versus prognostic-variable algebra that underlies every population-adjustment method,
then `MAIC.v`, the first file that puts the abstract `E` and an abstract `Var` to work together on the
effective-sample-size bound. From there the reading route of @sec-coqread-files orders the remaining
files by difficulty. The conceptual counterpart to all of this remains Chapter 30: this appendix teaches
you to verify and read the proofs on your own machine, while @sec-coq-map records, theorem by theorem,
what each of them certifies.
